content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.65. The evidence is weak and the call could go either way.

**How the tasks work:** each logic rule is a two-input Boolean function (OR, NOR, AND, NAND) applied to features chosen by the sensory rule. The motor rule then turns true or false into a pair of buttons. That means two tasks can share rules and give completely different responses, so "number of new rules" and "how much the outputs overlap" can be pulled apart.

**Design:** I trained on three tasks that share no rules: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested held-out tasks:

| Task | New rules | Most rules shared with one trained task | Output overlap | Mean examples (n) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 2 | 0.75 | 23.7 (21) |
| L1-S2-M3 | 0 | 1 | 0.625 | 26.7 (21) |
| L1-S4-M1 | 2 | 2 | 0.625 | 32.6 (8) |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 0 | 0.19 | 40.2 (6) |

**Why holistic:**
- **Against part-based:** it predicts the task with no new rules (L1-S2-M3) should be clearly cheaper than the one with a new rule (L1-S1-M4). It came out slightly more expensive. That is about 2 standard errors away from the gap part-based would expect.
- **Against holistic:** L1-S2-M3 was cheaper than L1-S4-M1 even though their output overlap is the same. That is only about 1 standard error, so it counts for less.
- **Noise:** results were very noisy (single tests on the same task ranged from 1 to 48 examples, SD about 14), so no comparison was decisive.

I used 59 of the 60 budget units.
